meta.title: Who really said "When Two Men in Business Always Agree, One of Them Is Unnecessary"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Henry Ford. The chewing-gum magnate William Wrigley Jr. said it in a 1931 magazine interview about why he refused to employ yes-men.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'When Two Men in Business Always Agree, One of Them Is Unnecessary'?
meta.ogDescription: The Ford credit is a 21st-century invention. William Wrigley Jr. said it in The American Magazine in March 1931 — ten months before he died.

answer.label: Not Henry Ford — actually William Wrigley Jr.
answer.authorDates: 1861–1932 · American chewing-gum manufacturer; founder of the Wm. Wrigley Jr. Company and owner of the Chicago Cubs
answer.sourceLine: Wrigley said it in an interview with Neil M. Clark published in The American Magazine for March 1931, under the title “Spunk Never Cost a Man a Job Worth Having”. His words there were shorter than the version in circulation — “When two men always agree, one of them is unnecessary” — and the point was that he wanted employees who would argue with him. Henry Ford’s name was not attached to it until 2003.

source.excerpt: Business is built by men who care—care enough to disagree, fight it out to a finish, get facts. When two men always agree, one of them is unnecessary.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ concludes: “QI suggests that William Wrigley Jr. should be credited with the words recorded in The American Magazine in 1931. QI further suggests that the saying should not be assigned to Ezra Pound or Henry Ford.”

The earliest instance is dated and paginated: The American Magazine, vol. 111 no. 3, March 1931, p. 63, in Neil M. Clark’s interview “Spunk Never Cost a Man a Job Worth Having”, per Quote Investigator ↗. The saying was reprinted within months — a Pennsylvania newspaper in August 1931, an Illinois one in October 1932 — and each time it is Wrigley’s.

The credit stayed with Wrigley for decades. Quote Investigator records Reader’s Digest printing it in July 1940 as “When two men in a business always agree, one of them is unnecessary — William Wrigley, Jr.”, the 1964 compilation Distilled Wisdom giving it to him in the modern wording, and the Forbes Scrapbook of Thoughts on the Business of Life carrying it in 1968 ↗.

The Ford attribution has no earlier life at all: Quote Investigator dates its first appearance to a 2003 book, The Laws of Software Process, in the form “Whenever two people always agree, one of them is unnecessary”. Neither the Wikiquote page for Henry Ford ↗ nor his Wikipedia biography ↗ carries the line in any form.
source.excerptNote: As reproduced by Quote Investigator from The American Magazine, March 1931. Note that the original has no “in business”: that phrase enters later, and the wording most often quoted today matches a 1964 compilation rather than the 1931 interview.

source.rightsNote: This one falls on the wrong side of the line by a matter of months: United States copyright can still reach works first published from 1931 onward, and the interview appeared in March 1931. We have therefore classified it conservatively as in-copyright. We did not verify whether the magazine’s copyright was renewed, which for a periodical of that period it may well not have been.

author.name: William Wrigley Jr.
author.heading: About William Wrigley Jr.
author.metaLine: 1861–1932 · American chewing-gum manufacturer; founder of the Wm. Wrigley Jr. Company and majority owner of the Chicago Cubs
author.bio: William Mills Wrigley Jr. built one of the great American consumer brands almost by accident, discovering that the chewing gum he gave away as a sales premium was more wanted than the soap and baking powder it was meant to promote. He founded the Wm. Wrigley Jr. Company in 1891, bought control of the Chicago Cubs by 1921 and had their ballpark named after him in 1926, and bought Santa Catalina Island outright in 1919. He died in Phoenix in January 1932.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The line is a favourite of management writing, which is exactly why it keeps changing owners: each retelling reaches for a bigger name than the last, and the gum manufacturer who actually said it is not the name anyone reaches for.

items.why: Quote Investigator finds the Ford credit no earlier than 2003, in The Laws of Software Process, and states there is “no substantive support” for it. Ford died in 1947. The line is absent from his Wikiquote page ↗, which collects both his sourced and his disputed quotations.
This one is newer still — Quote Investigator dates it to an Inc. magazine article in 2014, and gives it the same verdict as the Ford credit. Pound died in 1972.

Wrigley’s recorded words in 1931 are “When two men always agree, one of them is unnecessary.” The phrase “in a business” appears in Reader’s Digest in 1940 and the now-standard “in business” in a 1964 compilation, both still crediting Wrigley, per Quote Investigator ↗.

Interviewed by Neil M. Clark for The American Magazine under the title “Spunk Never Cost a Man a Job Worth Having”, Wrigley was making a hiring argument: he wanted people who would “care enough to disagree, fight it out to a finish, get facts.” He died the following January ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: It belongs to William Wrigley Jr., said in March 1931 about the kind of people he wanted working for him — and to Henry Ford only since 2003.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The line is usually quoted as a piece of hard-nosed executive wisdom about redundancy. In its original setting it is nearly the opposite: an argument for job security for people who argue back. The article’s title was “Spunk Never Cost a Man a Job Worth Having”, and Wrigley’s point was that the employee who disagrees is the one worth keeping.
That inversion is what the misattribution costs. Detached from the interview, the sentence sounds like a threat to whoever agrees; attached to it, it is a promise to whoever does not.
detailsBody: Wrigley had earned the right to the opinion. He arrived in Chicago in 1891 with, by Wikipedia’s account, thirty-two dollars, selling scouring soap and giving away baking powder as a premium, then giving away chewing gum as a premium for the baking powder, until he noticed which of the three people actually wanted. The company he built from that observation still bears his name.

He was also, by 1921, the majority owner of the Chicago Cubs, whose ballpark was renamed for him in 1926 and still is. The March 1931 interview came near the end: he died in Phoenix in January 1932, ten months after it appeared.
context.pull: Not a threat to the one who agrees — a promise to the one who does not.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator dates the earliest instance to The American Magazine, vol. 111 no. 3, March 1931, p. 63, in Neil M. Clark's article "Spunk Never Cost a Man a Job Worth Having", with Wrigley saying "When two men always agree, one of them is unnecessary."
Quote Investigator states there is no substantive support for crediting the saying to Ezra Pound or Henry Ford, and concludes William Wrigley Jr. should be credited.

The Henry Ford attribution first appears in 2003 in The Laws of Software Process as "Whenever two people always agree, one of them is unnecessary"; the Ezra Pound attribution first appears in a 2014 Inc. magazine article.

Reader's Digest, July 1940, printed "When two men in a business always agree, one of them is unnecessary" credited to William Wrigley, Jr.; the 1964 compilation Distilled Wisdom carries the modern wording, also credited to Wrigley.

William Mills Wrigley Jr. lived 30 September 1861 to 26 January 1932, founded the Wm. Wrigley Jr. Company in 1891, was majority owner of the Chicago Cubs by 1921 with their ballpark renamed for him in 1926, and bought Santa Catalina Island in 1919.
The Wikiquote page for Henry Ford does not contain the phrase "one of them is unnecessary" or any version of this saying.
Henry Ford lived 30 July 1863 to 7 April 1947, founded the Ford Motor Company in 1903, and his Wikipedia biography does not contain this saying.
The Wm. Wrigley Jr. Company was founded on 1 April 1891 in Chicago by William Wrigley Jr. and is a chewing gum and candy company.
